article_title: The Design and Implementation of the Akamai Maui Short Course
citation: Ryan Montgomery, Dave Harrington, Sarah Sonnett, Mark Pitts, Isar Mostafanezhad, Mike Foley, Eddie Laag, and Lisa Hunter. (2010). The Design and Implementation of the Akamai Maui Short Course. ASP Conference Series. https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.4458
title: Adaptive Optics Workbench activity: three engineering-challenge stations on a working AO system
description: The final AMSC inquiry is a series of three engineering challenge stations built around an adaptive optics system, whose stated objectives include to "Develop systems thinking by recognizing that a complex tool can be broken down into simpler components that work together as shown by block diagrams" and to troubleshoot, recognize trade-offs, and use feedback concepts. Station 1 has students measure focal-point deviation and invert measurements to deduce a hidden mirror's shape (an analogy to wavefront sensing); Station 2 asks students to improve an aberrated image via stopping down or phase-conjugate correction; Station 3 has students trace the optical path of a working AO workbench and produce a block diagram.
requirements: An AO workstation with wavefront sensor, computer and deformable mirror
Ray boxes, lenses and low-cost optical materials for the challenge stations
Prior student practice drawing ray diagrams from earlier inquiries
constraints: Real-world AO systems are complex and use expensive components (∼10-30k); the course version is an introductory-level demonstrator
target_learners: early-undergraduate STEM students preparing for technical internships
target_learning_goals: systems thinking, troubleshooting, experimental design, and understanding of adaptive optics concepts such as wavefront sensing, feedback and phase conjugation
examples: Groups rotate through three 50-minute stations and report out with posters describing how their station's content fits the AO system's internal functions.
key_sources: Ryan Montgomery, Dave Harrington, Sarah Sonnett, Mark Pitts, Isar Mostafanezhad, Mike Foley, Eddie Laag, and Lisa Hunter. (2010). The Design and Implementation of the Akamai Maui Short Course. ASP Conference Series. https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.4458

article_title: Teaching Optics and Systems Engineering With Adaptive Optics Workbenches
citation: D. M. Harrington, M. Ammons, Lisa Hunter, Claire Max, Mark Hoffmann, Mark Pitts, J. D. Armstrong. (2010). Teaching Optics and Systems Engineering With Adaptive Optics Workbenches. ASP Conference Series. https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.4463
title: Adaptive optics workbenches as fully functional optical systems for teaching
description: Four AO workbenches were funded, designed and constructed by institutions associated with the Center for Adaptive Optics, the Professional Development Program and the Institute for Scientist and Engineer Educators. Each is a functioning optical system that creates a blurred beam, senses the blur with a wavefront sensor, and corrects it with a deformable mirror. As the article states, "Adaptive optics workbenches are fully functional optical systems that can be used to illustrate and teach a variety of concepts and cognitive processes." They have been used in summer schools, classrooms, staff training and public demonstrations, from first-year undergraduate explorations to professional-level training.
requirements: A functioning AO system with laser source, aberrator, deformable mirror, wavefront sensor, lenslet array and science camera, plus software control of the DM
constraints: Design and performance capabilities differ across the four workbenches, and the actual design influences which activities can be run
examples: The CfAO workbench participates in the annual AO Summer School; the MCC workbench is used in ECET undergraduate coursework; the IfA Maui workbench is used in new four-year Engineering Technology classes
key_sources: D. M. Harrington, M. Ammons, Lisa Hunter, Claire Max, Mark Hoffmann, Mark Pitts, J. D. Armstrong. (2010). Teaching Optics and Systems Engineering With Adaptive Optics Workbenches. ASP Conference Series. https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.4463

article_title: Teaching Optics and Systems Engineering With Adaptive Optics Workbenches
citation: D. M. Harrington, M. Ammons, Lisa Hunter, Claire Max, Mark Hoffmann, Mark Pitts, J. D. Armstrong. (2010). Teaching Optics and Systems Engineering With Adaptive Optics Workbenches. ASP Conference Series. https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.4463
title: AO workbench activity progression from systems outlining to optimization
description: The article organizes workbench teaching as a progression of activity types of increasing depth: a short systems outline/block-diagramming warm-up, multi-station investigations of sensing and correction, a re-alignment design challenge, and finally systems optimization with quantitative performance measurement. Content spans what the authors list as "optical alignment, collimation, beam expansion and compression, re-imaging, optical relays, phase conjugation, aberration, wavefronts, wavefront sensing and beam correction" alongside systems engineering topics such as feedback loops and characterization. The same hardware supports activities from short undergraduate investigations to thorough professional-level engineering challenges.
requirements: A functioning AO workbench whose subsystems can be treated independently, with one control loop between the DM and the WFS
constraints: Activity types are heavily dependent on the content and cognitive processes to be taught, and on the workbench design and DM capability
target_learning_goals: optical concepts such as conjugation and relays
examples: At the AMSC a three-hour investigation used three stations: wavefront sensing, wavefront correction, and systems characterization; at the AOSS the lab section spans three labs within a five-day course
key_sources: D. M. Harrington, M. Ammons, Lisa Hunter, Claire Max, Mark Hoffmann, Mark Pitts, J. D. Armstrong. (2010). Teaching Optics and Systems Engineering With Adaptive Optics Workbenches. ASP Conference Series. https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.4463

article_title: The Adaptive Optics Summer School Laboratory Activities
citation: Ammons, S. M., Severson, S., Armstrong, J. D., Crossfield, I., Do, T., Fitzgerald, M., Harrington, D., Hickenbotham, A., Hunter, J., Johnson, J., Johnson, L., Li, K., Lu, J., Maness, H., Morzinski, K., Norton, A., Putnam, N., Roorda, A., Rossi, E., & Yelda, S. (2011). The Adaptive Optics Summer School Laboratory Activities. ASP Conference Series, Vol. 436. https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.2015
title: AO Demonstrator: a standalone closed-loop adaptive optics system for hands-on realignment and closed-loop operation practice
description: The AO Demonstrator is a self-enclosed, standalone closed-loop adaptive optics system running at 30 Hz with an AgilOptics mirror, built entirely for educational and demonstrative purposes. It comprises a 37-actuator drumhead deformable mirror, an 8x8 Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor, input laser, two sets of reimaging optics, and a science camera whose output is shown in real time on a screen. Groups of 3-4 students realign the system after lenses are removed and then achieve good closed-loop performance; advanced groups vary control loop parameters or insert new distortions such as eyeglasses or plastic sheets.
requirements: A facilitator must be able to reset the system so that "the ease of realigning the AO Demonstrator ensured that the majority of groups succeeded in this task."
target_learners: graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in astronomy, vision science, optics, and laser communications
target_learning_goals: recognizing components of an adaptive optics system
operating a working AO system in closed loop
examples: Groups of 3-4 students were shown the operating Demonstrator's image quality, then realigned it after reimaging lenses were removed, then achieved closed-loop performance after automatic calibration.
